name: Question 17
problem:
For the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1$ calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ as a function of $\theta .$

| $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ | $=$ | {{field-1}} |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ |
worked_solution:
To find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}
$$

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Using the fact that $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1,$ we get

$$
x=(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate ${x}^{′}(\theta )$ and ${y}^{′}(\theta ):$ 

- First, we compute the derivative of $x$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(\theta ) & ={((\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute the derivative of $y$ with respect to $\theta $ using the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(\theta ) & ={((\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{′} \\  & ={(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)}^{′}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{′} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To find dydx, we use the formula for differentiating parametric curves:

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ)

First, we recall that to convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ.

Using the fact that r=sin⁡θ+1, we get

x=(sin⁡θ+1)cos⁡θ,y=(sin⁡θ+1)sin⁡θ.

To compute our derivative, we first need to calculate x′(θ) and y′(θ):

  • First, we compute the derivative of x with respect to θ using the product rule: x′(θ)=((sin⁡θ+1)cos⁡θ)′=(sin⁡θ+1)′⋅cos⁡θ+(sin⁡θ+1)⋅(cos⁡θ)′=(cos⁡θ)⋅cos⁡θ+(sin⁡θ+1)⋅(−sin⁡θ)=cos⁡θcos⁡θ−(sin⁡θ+1)sin⁡θ

  • Then, we compute the derivative of y with respect to θ using the product rule: y′(θ)=((sin⁡θ+1)sin⁡θ)′=(sin⁡θ+1)′⋅sin⁡θ+(sin⁡θ+1)⋅(sin⁡θ)′=(cos⁡θ)sin⁡θ+(sin⁡θ+1)cos⁡θ

Therefore,

dydx=y′(θ)x′(θ)=cos⁡θsin⁡θ+(sin⁡θ+1)cos⁡θcos⁡θcos⁡θ−(sin⁡θ+1)sin⁡θ.
